name: Cheek implants

lead: Cheek implants are solid synthetic shapes placed on or under the cheekbone to make the midface more projected or fuller. People use them for flat cheekbones, asymmetry, ageing and facial feminisation, and looksmaxxers want higher, more angular cheekbones.

The implant sits over the malar bone, below it (submalar) or both, and fixed with sutures or screws, adding permanent volume unless removed. Reviews of the surgical literature report high patient satisfaction, with the evidence mostly retrospective series.

paras: Placement is through the mouth under anaesthesia. Users choose between malar and submalar shapes and between stock and custom implants. Swelling takes weeks to settle, and the shape is judged after healing. Some people also use fillers or fat as a softer alternative.

A 2025 meta-analysis of 3,701 patients found a 7.4 percent complication rate for malar implants (10.7 percent across facial implants), with high heterogeneity. Reported issues include infection, displacement, visible prominence and asymmetry. They are surgical devices placed by a surgeon.

angle.text: Cheek implants add projection over the cheekbone, giving higher, more angular cheekbones that are visible after healing. Reviews report high satisfaction, and the evidence is mostly case series rather than trials.

lead: Cheek implants, also called malar or submalar implants, are solid alloplastic (synthetic) devices placed over or beneath the cheekbone to increase midface projection or fullness. For appearance, a malar implant adds height and definition at the cheekbone, producing a higher, more angular contour, and a submalar implant fills a flat or hollow area below it for a fuller cheek. They are used to correct congenital cheekbone underdevelopment, asymmetry and age-related volume loss, and in gender-affirming facial surgery, and they are discussed in looksmaxxing communities as a way to obtain higher or more angular cheekbones.[1][2][3]

The usual materials are silicone and porous high-density polyethylene (sold as Medpor), with expanded PTFE (Gore-Tex) also used. The implant is typically inserted through an incision inside the mouth and stabilised with sutures or screws.[1][4][5] Reviews describe the result as permanent but reversible, since the implant can be removed.[1]

Published evidence consists mainly of reviews and case series rather than randomised trials. A 2022 review reported high patient satisfaction and low complication rates,[3] while a 2025 meta-analysis of 48 studies reported an overall complication rate of 10.7% for facial skeletal implants and 7.4% for malar implants specifically, with substantial heterogeneity between studies.[6] A 2018 systematic review found that malar implants had a high incidence of prominence problems.[4] A 2008 review noted that enthusiasm for cheek implants appeared to be declining in favour of soft-tissue approaches such as fat and fillers.[7]

Within looksmaxxing, cheek implants sit in the group of procedures often called hardmaxxing, alongside jaw and chin implants, rhinoplasty and osteotomies.[8] Forum discussion centres on implant shape, custom designs from CT scans, surgeon choice and travel for combined procedures.[9][10][11]
infobox: Intraoral incision near the upper gum line[5]
Sedation or general anaesthesia; about 1 to 2 hours[5]
Removable, but porous materials may integrate with tissue[1][5]

paras: The cheekbone (zygomatic, or malar, region) is one of the features that shapes the midface in both frontal and three-quarter views. Cheek augmentation is the group of procedures intended to emphasise this area; Wikipedia lists a solid implant over the cheekbone, injection of the patient's own fat, an injectable filler and, rarely, cuts to the zygomatic bone as the options, and notes that the procedure is often combined with a face lift or chin augmentation.[5]

Surgeons describe alloplastic malar augmentation as a reliable way to obtain permanent but reversible volume enhancement that corrects the changes of facial ageing, hypoplasia and congenital malar asymmetry. The amount of augmentation chosen depends on how severe the bony hypoplasia or soft-tissue volume loss is.[1]

Cheek implants are grouped by where they sit. Malar (shell) implants rest on the cheekbone and are intended to raise and sharpen the cheekbone contour; Wikipedia calls this the most common shape. Submalar implants sit lower and fill a hollow, flat or gaunt midface, producing a rounder cheek. Combined malar/submalar implants address both areas.[5][9]

Silicone is the most common material and is smooth and easier to remove. Porous high-density polyethylene and ePTFE are inert and integrate with surrounding tissue, which can anchor the implant but, in the case of polyethylene, may make later removal harder if a revision is needed.[4][5] Custom implants designed from CT scans are also produced, and are discussed heavily in online communities.[11][12]

Surgeons describe malar augmentation for patients with flat cheekbones, midface hypoplasia, congenital asymmetry, or volume loss from ageing.[1] An early series reported using perforated silicone implants to make the face appear more oval and youthful, and to treat congenital or traumatic cheek deficiencies.[13] A later review described implants as an occasional adjunct to orthognathic (jaw-moving) surgery, able to simulate the visual effect of osteotomies in people with skeletal deficiencies, while stating that implants are not a substitute for such surgery.[14]

Cheek augmentation is also a component of facial feminisation surgery, where high cheekbones and a full malar area are regarded as feminine features. The usual options in that setting are fillers, fat grafting and implants.[2][15] Fillers are customisable and reversible but need maintenance, fat grafting is abundant and biocompatible but has uncertain long-term retention, and implants are described as reliable but carry implant-related complications.[2] Wikipedia dates the modern field to 1982, when surgeon Douglas Ousterhout began developing facial feminisation procedures after a request from a colleague.[16] A 2019 study examined the safety of combining several facial procedures, including those on different tissue planes, in one setting for transgender facial feminisation patients.[17]

Hyaluronic acid fillers and autologous fat are less invasive, adjustable and reversible, but require repeat treatment or have uncertain long-term retention.[2] Wikipedia notes that all injected materials are eventually resorbed, and describes hyaluronic acid products such as Restylane and Juvederm as the less expensive option.[5] The dermal filler literature lists bruising and swelling as common effects and rare but serious vascular events, and states that fillers are regulated as medical devices in the United States.[18] Midface lifts, barbed-suture techniques and thread-based approaches are other soft-tissue options discussed in the literature.[7][19] A rarely used operation cuts and repositions the zygomatic bone itself, mostly in reconstructive work.[5]

In general terms, the usual surgical approach is an incision inside the mouth near the upper gum line, through which the implant is slid into a pocket over the bone. Surgeons describe the transoral approach with suture stabilisation as the most common technique for alloplastic midface augmentation.[1][5] An incision near the eye is possible but less often chosen because of the visible scar risk.[5] The operation is usually performed under sedation or general anaesthesia, takes about one to two hours, and recovery is commonly quoted at about ten days.[5] The mouth carries more bacteria than the skin, and Wikipedia notes this raises infection risk with the intraoral route.[5]

A 2022 review of recent literature concluded that overall patient satisfaction with alloplastic malar implants is high and complication rates are low, and that outcomes are likely comparable with other modalities in suitable hands.[3] A 1999 five-year retrospective review of a silicone midface implant, a 1995 series of silicone malar augmentation and a one-year multicentre evaluation of preformed augmentation shapes (including malar implants) are among the older clinical series.[20][21][22]

Most evidence is retrospective, with variable follow-up, from 2 weeks to 15 years in one review.[4] The 2008 review of midfacial rejuvenation observed that enthusiasm for cheek implants seemed to be decreasing in favour of soft-tissue treatments.[7]

General surgical risks listed by Wikipedia include infection, bleeding, blood clots and swelling; asymmetry can follow uneven resorption, displacement or shifting, and temporary loss of sensation is common, with longer-lasting loss possible.[5]

The 2018 systematic review of 626 polyethylene and 365 silicone cases found more infections and displacements with silicone, more prominence problems with polyethylene, and low exposure and extrusion rates for both. It noted that malar implants had a high incidence of prominence problems compared with chin and mandibular implants.[4]

The 2025 meta-analysis of 3,701 patients who received 4,139 implants reported pooled complication rates of 10.7% for all facial skeletal implants, 15.1% for paranasal implants and 7.4% for malar implants, with high heterogeneity.[6] Reviews also list infection, migration and visibility as implant-related complications.[2]

An analysis of adverse events and malpractice litigation related to facial implant surgery has also been published.[23] A separate study examined whether online resources about cosmetic facial surgery are reliable and understandable to patients.[24]

Silicone malar implants were being used in the 1960s; a 1975 report in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery described 52 cases since 1964, using a perforated soft silicone implant to treat flat malar eminences and congenital or traumatic deficiencies.[13] Augmentation malarplasty was reported in the early 1980s,[25] and silicone and porous implants became standard materials in subsequent decades.[21][4] A 1995 series described malar augmentation with silicone implants,[21] and a 1997 French study examined coral blocks for cheek augmentation in 23 patients.[26]

Facial feminisation surgery developed from the 1980s and made cheek augmentation a routine component of gender-affirming care.[16][15] By the 2010s and 2020s, reviews were comparing implants with fillers and fat grafting, and custom CT-designed implants were being discussed alongside stock shapes.[2][3][11]

Human data are limited to retrospective series, a small number of prospective evaluations and systematic reviews. A one-year prospective multicentre evaluation of preformed implants included 82 patients receiving nasal, chin and malar implants.[22] A prospective study of coral blocks in 23 patients was published in 1997.[26] The 2018 systematic review pooled nine polyethylene studies (626 patients) and five silicone studies (365 patients),[4] and the 2025 meta-analysis pooled 48 studies,[6] with malar implants reported in 15 of those studies (853 of 1,788 patients in those studies, 45.8%). No randomised trial comparing malar implants with other cheek augmentation methods has been published.[3][4][6]

On looksmax.org, cheek implants are discussed as a hardmaxxing option for people who consider their midface flat or recessed, sometimes as an alternative to a Le Fort III osteotomy.[9] Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing places surgery such as jaw surgery and rhinoplasty in the 'hardmaxxing' category, in contrast with 'softmaxxing' practices such as skincare and grooming.[8]

Threads cover choosing surgeons, comparing off-the-shelf and custom designs, and combining implants with other procedures such as jaw and chin implants, brow lifts or fat grafts.[9][10][27][12] Members share 3D previews of planned implants for feedback, ask whether results look too large or too small, and post questions such as how long to wait after double-jaw surgery before adding infraorbital and malar implants.[28][29][30] Some members travel abroad for multi-procedure packages, and one poster reported a cost of about US$15,000 for a package that included cheek implants.[10]
Researchers have used Google Trends data to study public interest in facial cosmetic procedures and how it relates to surgical volumes.[31]

lore.intro: Cheek implants are discussed on looksmax.org as one of several midface hardmaxxing options, with debate over implant type, design and surgeon choice, and with 3D design previews and before-and-after images shared for feedback.[9][28][27]

claims.claim: Most cheek implants are the 'apple cheek' submalar type, which gives a bloated look, while malar implants give a defined, angular look.
Custom-designed implants are better than off-the-shelf implants.
Cheek implants can approximate the effect of a Le Fort III midface advancement.
Implants are a safe and permanent option when done by a skilled surgeon.
Men should avoid submalar implants; submalar augmentation is for women.
Implants are reversible, so a bad result can be undone.
Multi-procedure packages abroad are a practical way to get implants and other work done at once.

timeline.event: A surgical series begins using perforated silicone malar implants (reported 1975).[13]
Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery publishes a 52-case report on malar implants for facial appearance.[13]
Augmentation malarplasty is described in Archives of Otolaryngology; facial feminisation surgery begins to be developed around the same year.[25][16]
A series on malar augmentation with silicone implants is published.[21]
A French prospective study evaluates coral blocks for cheek augmentation in 23 patients.[26]
A five-year review of a silastic midfacial malar implant is published.[20]
A one-year multicentre evaluation of preformed facial implants, including malar shapes, is published.[22]
A review notes declining enthusiasm for cheek implants relative to soft-tissue treatments.[7]
A review describes the state of the art in facial feminisation surgery.[15]
Systematic review compares polyethylene and silicone facial implants; adverse-event and litigation analysis published.[4][23]
Reviews of alloplastic malar implants and of cheek augmentation in gender-affirming surgery are published.[2][3]
Meta-analysis of 3,701 patients reports a 7.4% complication rate for malar implants.[6]
